9ee465f0: Buriti - a lightweight, accessible local LLM server in Rust
e46ee170: Buriti is a small local server written in Rust with a web UI in 34 languages. It runs GGUF models with llama.cpp or with its own pure-Rust CPU engine, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API for code editors. No telemetry.
cc77ec8c: Buriti logo: a buriti palm with orange fruit over green hills, next to the word buriti
87e9ffab: A lightweight, friendly local runner for AI models, accessible to everyone and adaptable to different computing and financial realities. A small local server in Rust with a web UI in 34 languages that runs GGUF models, with two engines to choose from: llama.cpp, or Buriti's own pure-Rust engine.
78d90179: One executable of about 5 MB. Your chats are stored encrypted on your machine. No telemetry: the network is used only when you click a download.
01d9c2ba: GitHub repository Build from source
55e5356b: Run open-source LLMs (Qwen, Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Phi) on your own computer, from a clean browser interface, without cloud accounts.
22f6ccfc: Buriti aims to make AI models accessible to everyone, especially people who are usually left out for lack of resources: one small native executable that adapts to the memory and processor you have, everything configurable from the web UI, and a choice of how the model is executed. Ollama was the inspiration and a guide for the start of the project.
ee6dad51: Server, own inference engine and build are all Rust. No Go, no cgo, no system libraries to install: TLS uses rustls, which is pure Rust.
2b1a517f: To use a model you already have, point Buriti at the .gguf path. Files are used where they are: nothing is uploaded or copied.
6253807a: Status: working and in active development. Tested on Windows 10 x64. Linux and macOS builds are expected to work but have not been tested yet. No pre-built binaries are published yet.
42b54377: Chat UI with a sidebar of past conversations, encrypted at rest.
f8182990: Model catalog with provider, release date, size, license, strengths and "best for" notes, plus a "recommended for your PC" hint. Or point Buriti at any .gguf already on disk.
86f4992d: Step-by-step first-run guide: choose an engine, choose a model, start chatting.
114716be: Settings in the UI: engine, model, CPU threads, context size, GPU layers, port.
6d3654b2: Buriti Code: an OpenAI-compatible API on 127.0.0.1 so editors can use the loaded model for chat and fill-in-the-middle autocomplete. Details below.
dac27670: Light and dark themes, a built-in tutorial and on-screen warnings for the usual pain points (weak PC, low RAM, SmartScreen, firewall, losing the history key).
d6a1b685: One executable: the web UI is embedded in the binary.
fffd5504: Downloads (models and the llama.cpp engine) accepted only when their SHA-256 matches.
22d9fb69: The catalog ships these models, all Q4_K_M with verified SHA-256 (see the README for the current list): Qwen 2.5 0.5B / 1.5B / 3B, Qwen 3 0.6B, Gemma 3 1B, Llama 3.2 1B / 3B, Phi-3.1 mini, Phi-3.5 mini, Phi-4-mini and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3. Check each model's license before commercial use: the Qwen 2.5 3B card is marked non-commercial (Qwen Research License) and Gemma has its own terms.
8a6dcd69: You pick the engine that runs the model. The own engine is an alternative to llama.cpp, not a replacement.
1b7ac078: llama-server, downloaded from the UI with a SHA-256 check and run as a child process. The fastest and most compatible option; the only route to GPU (Vulkan build, untested on real hardware).
64ae2367: Written from scratch in Rust and built into the executable: no download, no extra process. CPU only (AVX2/F16C on x86-64, NEON on ARM64). Matches llama.cpp's generation speed on several models (see Performance).
517cbb23: Architectures, and how each was checked against llama.cpp
0f147465: Tokens, chat-prompt ids and logits; F16 control
f5f787c9: F16 control on 0.6B. Qwen3 4B: top-1 matches, but numeric-only text differs more than expected (see below)
896be2fb: 1B validated; F16 control, including a 613-token text beyond the 512 sliding window
9de92443: Tokens, chat ids and logits on quantized files; no F16 control. Phi-4-mini had no end-to-end chat test in that round
daf7e6f0: yes (explicit kernels; generic fallback for other CPUs)
fdba1d92: implemented; validated only by emulation, cross-compilation and a runtime self-test. Speed unmeasured
38129abb: Vulkan build available; untested by the maintainer
b27da2d3: Not covered by validation: Qwen3 1.7B/8B and Gemma 3 4B and up use the same code but were not tested with real files. Context beyond about 8 thousand tokens was not exercised for the Phi longrope models.
bd4c26c3: Requirements: Rust (stable, via rustup) and a linker/C toolchain for your OS. There are no system libraries to install.
57c86e65: The maintainer uses the GNU toolchain with MinGW-w64. The MSVC build tools also work in principle, but that path has not been verified.
eb586bc3: The executable icon is embedded at build time by build.rs (needs windres from MinGW, or rc.exe with MSVC). If the icon step fails the build still succeeds, only without the icon. Because the executable is not code-signed yet, Windows SmartScreen or your antivirus may warn on first run.
29d3949e: Untested: these commands follow the standard Rust tooling but have not been executed by the maintainer. Reports are welcome.
75a18418: Start buriti. Your browser opens at http://127.0.0.1:8421/#token=... (the console prints the same URL). The token changes on every start.
e6d67975: In the "Let's get started" card choose an engine (download llama.cpp, verified with SHA-256, or use Buriti's own), then a model from the catalog or a .gguf from your disk.
456b2f31: Start the engine and chat. Next time the engine starts by itself.
8491f676: A first release build takes a few minutes (about 5.5 minutes on a 2-core laptop, because of LTO) and yields an executable of about 5 MB that runs from any folder. A plain cargo build is also optimized (opt-level = 3), because the engine is about 20 times slower without optimization. Stop with Ctrl+C; the engines stop too.
cbdff777: Day-to-day settings live in the UI. These environment variables are for deployment and development:
c7a088e9: Data folder (default: buriti-data next to the executable).
77f471b7: Force the web UI / API port (default 8421; fails with a clear message if busy). Without it Buriti reuses the last port it used and, if that is busy, takes the next free one and says so in the console.
f2299050: Path to a llama-server binary to use instead of the downloaded one. Deliberately not editable from the web UI.
949f8d04: Path of the history encryption key.
3b5d78e1: If set, do not open the browser on start.
520d98a2: If set to 1, the own engine prints timing per weight format and per phase to stderr.
6429209f: Where things are stored: buriti-data/ holds models/, engine/, history/, settings.json and engine.log. The history key is kept in your user profile, not next to the chats (%APPDATA%\Buriti\key.bin on Windows, ~/.config/Buriti/key.bin on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/Buriti/key.bin on macOS). If you lose this file, old conversations cannot be recovered.
3159fa91: A small axum server in front of an Engine trait with two implementations. The web UI and the editor API never need to know which one is active.
b5426ecc: The browser and code editors send HTTP requests to the Buriti server on 127.0.0.1 port 8421. The server uses an Engine trait with two implementations: the llama.cpp llama-server child process on 127.0.0.1 port 8081, or the own Rust engine running in process. Both read a GGUF model file.
0272f10e: Web (web/): plain HTML/JS embedded in the binary.
19a9e41d: Server (src/server.rs): /api routes behind middleware (session token and Host check); the OpenAI-compatible routes are under /v1.
0c7d8d4d: Engine (src/engine/): the Engine trait (start, stop, status, chat, complete) with LlamaServerEngine (child process) and NativeEngine (in process).
43a4790a: Download (src/download.rs): streaming downloads with SHA-256 verification; archives are extracted without running anything.
737ef74e: History (src/history.rs): one file per conversation, encrypted with ChaCha20-Poly1305, the conversation id as associated data.
92c558bb: Correctness before speed. Every kernel has a test against a float reference. The 1-, 4- and 8-activation kernels must give strictly identical results, and batched prefill must be bit-identical to token-by-token processing, KV-cache bytes included.
93395c20: Int8 activation quantization with integer dot products (the technique llama.cpp uses), explicit AVX2 kernels with a generic fallback, KV cache in f16, prefill in batches of 32 tokens.
b758b2de: GGUF is read through mmap with bounds checks everywhere: a malformed file produces an error, never a panic.
f06bedd0: Code that cannot be tested on the dev machine (ARM) only ships with emulation in tests, cross-compilation and a runtime self-test that falls back to the generic path.
188a3224: An OpenAI-compatible API so code editors can use the model loaded in Buriti for chat and inline autocomplete. "Buriti Code" is a product name.
aa545bdb: The API lives at http://127.0.0.1:8421/v1 (use the port printed at start-up), loopback only. Start the engine with a model first: requests made while it is not ready get HTTP 409.
e6fc622e: Raw text completion. With suffix the model fills the gap between prompt (code before the cursor) and suffix (code after it): fill-in-the-middle, which is how inline autocomplete works.
bba228b4: chat (bash quoting; macOS, Linux, Git Bash)
b8a6563c: The web UI's Buriti Code page shows these with your real URL and key filled in.
8c328dcc: Point the openai provider at Buriti with apiBase in ~/.continue/config.yaml (Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.continue\config.yaml):
1108ef8c: Settings | Tools | AI Assistant | Providers & API keys: enter the URL and the API key, click Test Connection, leave tool calling off, then assign the model to the features you want. Per JetBrains, inline code completion has a separate setting.
483ea1fb: Choose the OpenAI Compatible provider and enter the base URL, API key and model id. Cline is an agent that needs tool calling, which Buriti lacks, so expect limited results.
ccc6b4dd: Model choice: for autocomplete the UI suggests Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B (fast); for chat, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B or Qwen 3 4B. On weak CPUs the 7B is slow, so prefer the 1.5B for everything.
71a08ed3: No editor plugin has been tested end to end (Continue, Cline, JetBrains). The wire format follows the documentation; real interoperability is unverified.
2c7fa1a0: Not supported, and rejected with a clear error instead of being ignored: tool/function calling (tools), n > 1 and image content. No embeddings endpoint (so no codebase indexing), no usage and no logprobs.
206f087c: Requests are processed one at a time, and chat and autocomplete share the one loaded model.
3e981e2e: Fill-in-the-middle needs a model with FIM tokens; the Qwen2.5-Coder family works in both engines. Instruct variants tend to keep generating after the gap, base models stop cleanly, and editor plugins usually cut the output. FIM for other model families was not tested.
df580c4e: Autocomplete latency depends on your CPU. Measured once, with Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B on the i7-7500U: about 0.3 to 0.5 s of prefill for 15 to 20 tokens and about 14 tokens/s generation. Only viable with small models.
9acf9f29: Buriti Code is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by OpenAI, Microsoft/GitHub, JetBrains, Continue or Cline. Those names are used only to say which tools it works with.
7be41a4b: Every number here comes from the project's decision log, with the condition it was measured under. They are one machine and one CPU generation: treat them as indicative.
a8c0ecb4: Own engine vs llama.cpp (build b12606): Intel Core i7-7500U (2 cores / 4 threads, AVX2 only), 4 threads, CPU only, Q4_K_M unless noted, interleaved runs, 3 rounds, medians, a prompt of about 560 tokens, development build (opt-level 3, no LTO), measured on 2026-11-24
6903bb2e: Prefill is at or above llama.cpp on all 12 models (101 to 184%). Generation is within 91 to 109% of llama.cpp, so it is close but not ahead.
1c717d01: The weights of the Q4_K, Q6_K, Q8_0 and Q5_0 formats are repacked into interleaved rows when the model loads. The earlier table on this page, with 66% and 69% prefill for the 1.5B class, is replaced by this one.
459bd971: The measuring laptop throttles when hot: the llama.cpp baseline itself fell from about 82/28 tok/s (prefill/generation, Qwen 0.5B) cold to about 57/19 hot. That is why every comparison is interleaved and run cold.
4fd3163a: Not measured: Ollama's own overhead, ARM64 speed, any CPU other than this one (no AVX-VNNI or AVX-512 here), long contexts (the prompt is about 560 tokens), and, beyond a small sample, the quality of the repacked Q8_0 and Q5_0 paths against llama.cpp. Phi-3.5 mini is supported but is not in this table: the measurements of its Q5_K path were too noisy to publish.
46ca552d: On an NVIDIA GeForce 940MX (4 GiB, Vulkan) with Qwen 2.5 0.5B Q4_K_M, the own engine reached 202 tok/s of prefill against 167 tok/s for the llama.cpp Vulkan build (121%), and 22.1 tok/s of generation against 24.4 (91%): medians of 3 interleaved rounds after a 60 second rest. It is one GPU and one model, so treat it as indicative.
a602bc7c: The own engine is validated against llama.cpp (b12606), not just by checking that the text looks right:
a065af59: Token ids: tokenization identical to llama.cpp's on 11 of 11 tricky texts, and the ids of rendered chat prompts identical on 3 of 3 conversations, for each supported family. Comparing ids catches errors that comparing text hides.
193fddc5: Logits against an unquantized F16 reference: maximum log-probability difference 0.0006 to 0.0021 on Qwen3 0.6B and 0.0027 to 0.0057 on Gemma 3 1B (0.0072 on a 613-token text), with an identical top-10. This proves the architecture.
2c30883e: Quantized models: the direct difference between engines is larger, typically 0.03 to 0.1 mean log-probability, mostly noise from int8 activation quantization shared by both engines. A planted bug (sliding window disabled) was caught by the long-text test, which is how the tests were checked to have teeth.
e440b0eb: A test suite compares every kernel with a float reference and checks that batched prefill is bit-identical to token-by-token processing.
b3ec91f7: Known caveats: Mistral 7B and Phi-3 were checked only on quantized files. Phi-4-mini quantized shows a larger gap (mean 0.08 to 0.25, max 0.72) and has no F16 control. For Qwen3 4B, numbers-only text differed by 0.65 on average (0.24 with float activations), so its quality on numeric text on the own engine is not proven. BF16 weights differ from llama.cpp by 0.02 to 0.066, worse than F16; the likely cause (llama.cpp rounding activations to BF16) was not proven by experiment.
e0977003: The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Each start creates a random session token, sent in the URL fragment and as an X-Buriti-Token header. The Host header is checked to block DNS-rebinding attacks.
de3912cf: Models and the llama.cpp engine are accepted only if the SHA-256 matches: the catalog hash for models, the release digest for the engine. Archives are extracted without running anything; zip-slip is blocked.
68a60d92: Chats are encrypted with ChaCha20-Poly1305. The key lives in your user profile, not beside the files. This stops casual opening or copying of the folder; it does not protect against someone who already controls your user session.
da3c411b: Compared in constant time, plus a loopback Host check and no CORS headers. Any program of yours that can read the key file can use the model (it spends CPU; it cannot read files or run anything).
55d713ca: Model files are untrusted input: the GGUF parser checks bounds everywhere.
5e361dd1: Text you type is never interpreted as a special token, so chat delimiters cannot be injected.
a43faabf: No telemetry. The network is used only when you click a download. This project site makes no external requests either: no analytics, no CDN, no web fonts.
dc4e9efc: The interface is available in 34 languages; a missing key falls back to English. The translations are AI-generated and need review by native speakers. The least certain are Yoruba, Amharic, Oromo, Igbo, Shona, Hausa, Zulu, Khmer, Papiamento and Haitian Creole. Long per-model catalog notes exist in English, Portuguese and Spanish and fall back to English elsewhere. A native-speaker review is one of the most useful contributions you can make.
59cb1486: Tested mainly on one Windows 10 machine. Linux and macOS are untested, including the .tar.gz engine download and extraction.
13d0fec5: GPU (the Vulkan build of llama.cpp) has not been tested on real hardware.
d07e5029: The own engine is CPU only. On ARM64 the NEON kernels are validated by emulation, cross-compilation and a self-test (no ARM machine was available), so their speed is unmeasured.
1d985d98: Prefill speed for 1B to 3B models: kernels with fewer instructions per multiply-accumulate, AVX-VNNI, an LTO release build and re-measuring Llama 3.2 3B.
52a7d453: NEON: measure on real ARM (Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi 5); use sdot.
07310d8b: More architectures (Gemma 2, larger Gemma 3, Mistral Nemo/Small) and remaining quantizations (Q2_K, Q3_K, Q8_K, IQ*).
3639d5b2: Distribution: CI-built binaries (MSVC on Windows), optional master password or OS keystore for the history key, an updatable catalog.
92d4b703: GPU in the own engine via wgpu (Vulkan/Metal/DX12) and an installer.
4d8d0183: Record each design decision in docs/DECISIONS.md with what was measured and what was not covered.
ea8b457a: UI text goes in web/i18n*.js in all 34 languages, with placeholders such as {threads} kept intact.
832a827f: Write kernel tests against a float reference, and plant a bug on purpose to confirm a new test fails.
a8153c25: Validate new architectures by token ids and logits against llama.cpp (an F16 file should match to about 0.003), not by eyeballing output.
d1cdf3c0: When measuring speed, interleave runs with llama.cpp, run cold, repeat 3 or more times and report the condition; do not call noise a gain.
89ee24d6: Treat third-party code and binaries as untrusted: review before running anything.
2e744d82: Run the tests with cargo test (30 unit tests plus 7 ignored diagnostics). Issues, test reports from Linux, macOS and ARM machines, and translation reviews are all welcome on the GitHub repository.
